title: John Holt, on Understanding (part 1)
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane draws on a passage from John Holt's How Children Fail in which a student, Walter, gets right answers and plausible explanations on rate problems without understanding the underlying math. Holt's point is that teachers who accept an answer plus an explanation can be fooled by what he calls numeral shoving and word shoving. Kane connects this to a professional development session on having students write mathematical explanations, and admits he is now less confident that explanations demonstrate understanding. He separates two purposes for explanation: presenting work clearly to others, and exploring a question collectively to understand a concept. His worry is that explanation becomes rote chatter, teaching students that a right answer must come with a ritual sentence rather than with sense-making. The post is brief and leans heavily on the Holt excerpt, but Kane's distinction is a useful one for teachers.
points: A student can produce correct answers and fluent explanations while understanding nothing, so neither is reliable evidence of understanding.
Holt's idea that students learn they need the right answer plus the right chatter describes how explanation requirements can become ritual.
Kane distinguishes explanation as clear presentation of work from explanation as collective exploration of an open question.
Students who think that knowing the rules produces the right answer will treat explanations as another rule to follow.
quotes: Most teachers would have assumed, as I would have once, that when he got the 15-minutes problem, he knew what he was doing. Even the skeptical would have been convinced when he gave his explanation about the 30-minutes problem. Yet in each case he showed that he had not really understood what he was doing, and it is not at all certain that he understands yet.

Might not a child feel, as Walter obviously did, that in this school you not only have to get the right answer, but you also have to have the right explanation to go with it; the right answer, and the right chatter.

That's the chatter that Holt refers to, and it's a waste of students' time, and what students are learning isn't math--they're learning that when you solve a problem, you don't just need a right answer, you need to say this thing about a complete sentence and name the thing we talked about in class that day.

I really worry about this. My students' mindsets about math are largely--to quote David Cox--"If I know the rules, then I can do the math". And more specifically, if I know the rules, I can find the right answer.
What was his strategy here? Certainly he was numeral shoving. More than that he was making up a fairly sensible sounding explanation of how he was doing the problem.
